A throttleable rocket engine designed to turn the MiG-21 into a super-high-performance rocket interceptor. It proved successful in tests, but the destruction of the only prototype due to an engine explosion and the increasing performance of jet-powered aircraft led to the project being abandoned.
The ullage motor of the Saturn V S-II stage. Attaches to the upper part of the S-II interstage in sets of 4 to 8.
Ullage motor for the S-IV and S-IVB. Can be jettisoned after use to save weight.
Los Alamos "Small Engine" Atomic Rocket Motor
The Los Alamos "Small Engine" was a compact nuclear thermal rocket derived from the PEWEE core. Designed to be used as a Space Shuttle upper stage, it has a unique folding nozzle to reduce length.

The "SNTP-PFE" series is a 1000MW reactor. The reactor is a particle bed using metallic carbide coated uranium granules embedded in a graphite rod that hydrogen is passed through. This allows for power densities of up to 40MW/liter. Its core is capable of starting up five times. An integral Tungsten Boron Lithium Hydride composite shield is included and the whole assembly is regeneratively cooled. A secondary circuit runs the shut down gasses through a small heat engine to minimize fuel loss and provide basic alternator power. This engine should be mounted three to six meters from the closest fuel tank. Fuel should shield any crew and crew positions when running should be ten to fifteen meters from the engine. Additional shielding such as a water tank or high density fuel can somewhat reduce this amount. This rocket has impressive stats for its size (Nozzle Ae=100 Chamber Temp=3000 Ideal ISP=991 Reactor Power=1054MW(th) TWR=13.94 Chamber Pressure=6800kPa Ignitions =5 Tonnage including integral shadow shield:1.504tons ) The nozzle is a fixed ablatively cooled filament wound carbon-carbon design.

Derived from the Sprite, the Spectre was a rocket motor designed for the SR.53 interceptor, and to replace the Sprite for higher-performance JATO applications. It was tested extensively, both on the SR.53 prototypes and on the Vickers Valiant and Hadley-Page Victor, but improved jet engine performance and cancellation of the SR.53 and the SR.177 follow-on project resulted in the cancellation of the Spectre.
An early Soviet Hall Effect thruster, used on Soviet and Russian weather satellites.
The first ever operational ion thruster, the SPT-60 Hall Effect thruster was first used in 1971 on Soviet Meteor weather satellites.
A Hall effect ion thruster used on many commercial spacecraft for station keeping.
The SPT-140 is an enlarged SPT-100 created to power large, modern communications satellites.

A small monopropellant rocket motor, intended for JATO use to improve the takeoff performance of various aircraft. Developed directly from german JATO boosters captured during WW2, the Sprite incorporated improvements such as silver gauze catalyst beds, but was still a low-performance motor. The Super Sprite added a kerosene "afterburner" that injected small amounts of kerosene into the combustion chamber to increase performance.
The SR19 is an improved Minuteman second stage developed for the LGM-30F Minuteman II.
A mid-sized apogee kick motor used on ATS-1/2/3.
The SR73 is an improved Minuteman third stage developed for the LGM-30F Minuteman II.

The Titan IVB Solid Rocket Motor Upgrade (also known as the Upgraded Solid Rocket Motor or USRM), was developed with the goal of 25% more capacity than the Titan IVA with the UA1207 SRM. It achieved this through a more energetic propellant and a 3-segment composite case that carried more fuel and weighed less than the UA1207's 7-segment steel case. Burn time 150 seconds.

Developed from the RS-25 SSME, the Space Shuttle Booster Engine (SSBE) was a concept for a kerolox fueled Space Shuttle booster. The engine used three fuel-rich preburners, burning a mixture of LH2 and RP-1 to minimize coking. The LH2 was also used to cool the combustion chamber, allowing unmodified SSME components to be used.

The RS-25, also known as the Space Shuttle Main Engine (SSME), is a LH2/LOX fuel-rich staged combustion engine. Though complex and expensive, these engines provide very high performance and are extremely reliable. Three of these engines powered each Shuttle Orbiter and four power the core stage of the SLS.

The RS-25, also known as the Space Shuttle Main Engine (SSME), is a LH2/LOX fuel-rich staged combustion engine. This version uses an extendable nozzle, allowing the SSME to switch from a 50:1 sea level nozzle to a 150:1 vacuum nozzle mid-flight. Intended for SSTO use, where the extending nozzle would allow for the required performance at sea level and vacuum.

The RS-25, also known as the Space Shuttle Main Engine (SSME), is a LH2/LOX fuel-rich staged combustion engine. This version has an enormous 650:1 vacuum nozzle and has undergone extensive weight-reduction measures for use on a martian space tug.

The STAR 3 motor was developed and qualified in 2003 as the Transverse Impulse Rocket System (TIRS) for the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) program for JPL in Pasadena, CA. Three TIRS motors were carried on each of the MER landers. One of the TIRS motors was fired in January 2004 to provide the impulse necessary to reduce lateral velocity of the MER Spirit lander prior to landing on the Martian surface. The motor also has applicability for spin/despin and separation systems.

This STAR motor was developed and tested in January 2000 under a NASA Goddard Space Flight Center program for a low-cost, high mass fraction orbit adjust motor for use in deploying constellations of very small satellites (nanosatellites). The first static test of the STAR 4G prototype motor was conducted 8 months after program start. The motor is designed to operate at high chamber pressure and incorporates a noneroding throat insert to maximize specific impulse.

The STAR 5C rocket motor was initially designed and produced (1960-1963) under a contract with Martin Marietta. The STAR 5C is used to separate the second stage from the trans-stage on the Titan II missile and Titan launch vehicle. The current version was qualified for use in 1976, replacing the earlier main propellant grain with TP-H-3062.

The STAR 5D rocket motor was designed and qualified to serve as the Rocket-Assisted Deceleration (RAD) motor on the Mars Pathfinder mission. Three of these motors were fired to slow the Pathfinder spacecraft to near-zero velocity before bouncing on the surface of Mars.

The STAR 6B rocket motor was developed for spin-up and axial propulsion of re-entry vehicles. The design incorporates an aluminum case and a carbon-phenolic nozzle assembly. The STAR 6B was qualified in 1984 and first flew in 1985.

The STAR 8 was developed and qualified as the Rocket Assisted Deceleration (RAD) motor for the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) program. The motor is based on the STAR 5D motor technology developed for JPL’s Mars Pathfinder program. The STAR 8 first flew in January 2004 when three motors were used to decelerate each of the Spirit and Opportunity rovers for landing at Gusev Crater and Meridiani Planum on Mars.

The STAR 9 rocket motor was developed in 1993 on independent research and development funds to demonstrate a number of low-cost motor technologies. These included an integral aft polar boss/exit cone, two-dimensional carbon-carbon throat, and case-on-propellant manufacturing technique.
The Star 12A is a stretched Star 12 with improved propellant, for later, heavier satellites in the Keyhole series.
The Star 13 was developed in the mid-1960s as the braking motor for the AIMP program, and was used on Explorer 33 and 35.
The Star 13A was developed in the mid-1960s as an apogee motor for Thor-Burner II.

This orbit insertion motor incorporated the lightweight case developed for the STAR 13 with the propellant and nozzle design of the earlier TE-M-516 apogee motor. The motor case was stretched 2.2 inches to provide for increased propellant loading. This motor was used to adjust the inclination of a satellite from a Delta launch.
A small apogee kick motor used for geosynchronous satellites. It was used on the first geosynchronous satellite, Syncom 1.
A single STAR 15G motor, used in a variety of applications. This has a straight nozzle.
A small apogee kick motor for satellites, introduced in 1968 on Delta 57. Max thrust 12.34kN, burn time 18 seconds.

Apogee kick motor. Modifications: 175 mm straight section added to the Star 17. The 17A has been used for circularized orbits for the Skynet 1, NATO 1, and IMP-H & J satellites. This motor provides the high case safety factor required for this program. The TE-M-521-7 model used for several Air Force missions provides a typical safety factor with a 1.3 pound weight savings.

The lightweight external nozzle is a composite of graphite, plastic, and steel. The consumable pyrogen igniter is actuated by two 6-second-delay electrical initiators or two SBASI zero-time-delay initiators.

The STAR 24C is an improved variant of the STAR 24 solid rocket motor, designed for the International Ultraviolet Explorer mission. Features an increased propellant loading and higher chamber pressure compared to the baseline STAR 24 motor.

An apogee motor developed for the Canadian Communications Research Centre's Communications Technology Satellite. An offloaded version was qualified and flown successfully. With various propellant loadings and explosive transfer assemblies, it was used for the Broadcast Satellite Experiment, the Geostationary Meteorological Satellite, the Navigation Technology Satellite No. 2, the Global Positioning System Satellites, the P78-1 Satellite, and the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite.
An apogee kick motor developed by Morton Thiokol. Used by various small commsat busses.

Antares III is the third-generation third stage for Vought Corporation's Scout launch vehicle. The design incorporates an 89-percent-solids HTPB propellant in a Kevlar filament-wound case insulated with silica-filled EPDM rubber.
The STAR 37 is a vacuum solid rocket motor originally developed as a braking stage for the Surveyor lunar lander program. Later variants were used exclusively as apogee kick stages.

The STAR 37E is an improved version of the venerable STAR 37 solid rocket motor, featuring increased propellant loading, higher efficiency, and more vacuum thrust. It was first used on the Delta 1000 launch vehicle family as a third stage kick motor.

The STAR 37FM is an improved version of the venerable STAR 37 solid rocket motor, featuring increased propellant loading, higher efficiency, and more vacuum thrust. It was first used on the FTLSATCOM satellites as an apogee motor.

Also known as the Payload Assistance Module (PAM) B, this kick motor was used for Delta and STS launches to add extra impulse to the payload. This is the short-nozzle version. Maximum thrust 76.11kN, burn time 85 seconds.

The STAR 63, as part of the PAM DII upper stage, has been flown from the Space Shuttle. The motor utilizes a head-end web and a carbon-phenolic nozzle. The case material is a Kevlar-epoxy composite, through future motors would be made using a graphite-epoxy composite. Testing of STAR 63 series motors began in 1978 with completion of the PAM DII motor qualification in 1985. The first STAR 63D flight was from the Shuttle in November 1985 to place a defense communication satellite in orbit.

Developed for SpaceX Starlink satellites, this small but powerful hall effect thruster offers good thrust and moderate specific impulse. Uniquely, it was modified to run on Argon to reduce fuel costs.
The Space Transportation Booster Engine (STBE) was a late 1980s to early 1990s booster engine design using JP-4 and liquid oxygen as its propellants.
The Space Transportation Booster Engine (STBE) was a 1990s proposal for a highly reliable low cost booster engine for both expendable and reusable launch vehicles.

Stentor was developed as a two chamber booster-sustainer for the Blue Steel missile, with one chamber providing boost thrust and another smaller chamber providing sustainer thrust. This part represents the larger booster chamber. The smaller chamber was developed into the Gamma series of rocket engines, while the larger chamber was proposed for several projects, but ultimately never developed further.

The Space Transportation Main Engine was a hydrolox engine, ultimately cancelled in 1992. Rocketdyne was teamed with Aerojet and Pratt & Whitney on the STME, which would have powered the next generation of large launch vehicles.
A powerful hypergolic engine used in the launch abort system of the Dragon 2 capsule. Other potential applications include hypersonic deceleration and landing for crew and cargo modules.
A small apogee kick motor used for the Intelsat II series of geostationary satellites.
A small apogee kick motor used for the Intelsat III series of geostationary satellites.
A medium apogee kick motor used for the Intelsat IV and IVA series of geostationary satellites, as well as some early Comstar satellites.
A small apogee kick motor used for early SMS and GOES geostationary weather satellites.
A 100 kW Applied-Field MPD thruster in development at the University of Stuttgart Institute of Space Systems. It set a thruster efficiency record of 61.99% in 2019.

The Vernier System as used on the Surveyor Probes. It uses storable hypergolic propellants, has infinite restarts, is not subject to ullage, and is throttleable down to 30%. Historically 3 of them were used on the Surveyor probes which landed on the Moon.

The Viking lander Terminal Descent Engine (TDE). The lander had three such engines, which were used during the final 45 seconds or so of the descent to the surface of Mars. Multiple small exhaust nozzles are used to diffuse the exhaust plume to eliminate a recirculation zone that could contaminate spacecraft instrumentation and avoid potential extensive erosion of the landing site.
The Mercury retro motor, intended to deorbit the capsule. Place 3 on the Mercury Retropack. These were fired in sequence at five second intervals.

A small solid fueled booster originally used to power anti-shipping rockets during WW2. It was used as the kick stage on the WAC Corporal, the USA's first sounding rocket, and reused in a modified form for the Aerobee line of sounding rockets.
An early French solid rocket engine used for the first stage of the Topaze sounding rocket and second stage of the Diamant A and B launch vehicles.

An early 2000s atmospheric staged combustion kerolox engine developed as the booster engine for a Space Shuttle replacement as a part of the Space Launch Initiative program. High performance with reusability and throttling capabilities, but cancelled during prototype phase.
A small pressure-fed sustainer for MR-1 Meteo sounding rockets, developed in response to the American Aerobee. Used after a small solid booster.
4 segment strap-on booster for proposed Saturn IB derivatives. Burn time 115s.
5 Segment strap-on booster for Titan IIIC, IIID, IIIE, proposed for Saturn IB derivatives. Burn time 115s.
5.5 segment strap-on booster for Titan 34D and Commercial Titan III. Burn time 115s.

The UA1207 was used on the Titan IVA, which was developed to launch payloads that had been designed to fly on the Shuttle from Vandenberg. It was a 7-segment modification of the 5-segment UA1205 used on the Titan 3. Burn time 130 seconds.
Speculative 8 segment version of the UA107. Burn time 115s.
A Wasserfall derivative engine developed by German and French engineers after WW2 for the sounding rocket of the same name. It was the first French high altitude sounding rocket.

Developed as a "Super-Veronique", the Vexin is a large pressure-fed booster engine used on the Vesta and "Precious Stones" series of sounding rockets, as well as the Diamante and Europe launch vehicles. One of the largest pressure-fed engines ever flown, this engine is simple but low performance.

Based on the Ad Astra lab test article built to test the configuration to be flown on the ISS, the VASIMR engine is far more powerful than any other ion engine to this point. It will require about 200kW of power.

A high thrust hypergolic vacuum engine. Derived from the European Viking engines that were used on the early Ariane launch vehicles for booster or sustainer roles. ISRO adapted them as a vacuum engine for the second stage of the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) families.

A hypergolic booster engine developed for the European Ariane launch vehicle. Used as both a first stage engine and second stage engine when equipped with an extended nozzle. A version was also created for the Ariane 4 strap-on liquid boosters. Unremarkable performance, but good reliability.

Operational Viking variants with bell nozzles, used on the first stage of Ariane 1-4, and on the Ariane 4 strap-on liquid boosters. The Viking is a hypergolic booster engine developed for Ariane and used as both a first and second stage engine (when equipped with an extended nozzle). Unremarkable performance, but good reliability.
Vulcain is a gas-generator sustainer engine that was previously used on Ariane 5 and is now used on Ariane 6.
The first proper VASIMR engine built by Ad Astra, the VX-200SS (Steady State) is built for long-term operation at a wide range of ISP and thrust, with multiple propellant options.
The Waxwing was a small solid kick motor for circularizing payloads in orbit, used as a third stage on the Black Arrow launch vehicle in 1970-71. 29.4kN average thrust.

Developed to power the Wasserfall anti-aircraft missile, the Wasserfall Booster was essentially a 1/4 scale A-4. Designed to be cheap and able to launch on short notice, it used a simple pressure-fed feed system and was powered by explosives-grade nitric acid and liqufied coal. Although the rocket worked well, difficulty in developing a guidance system that could accurately engage aircraft proved impossible with the technology available. Post-war, it was tested by both American and Soviet engineers. Soviet engineers developed improved versions for the R-101, but were also unable to develop a practical guidance system for anti-aircraft use, and instead converted it into a ballistic missile, creating the R-11 (Scud).

This 3-channel thruster was designed for operation up to 250 kW of discharge power at specific impulses ranging from 1800–3500 seconds on xenon propellant and up to 5000 seconds on krypton, all with state of the art total efficiencies in excess of 60%.
A very early kerolox gas generator booster engine used on the Vanguard launch vehicle.

Xenon Ion Propulsion System, 25 cm. A small gridded ion thruster developed by L-3 technologies to act as a stationkeeping thruster for commercial satellites. Currently used on the Boeing 601 and 702 satellite busses. Mass/power ratio: 3.56 kg/kW.

The Reaction Motors XLR10 was an early rocket developed to power the Viking sounding rocket. Intended to replace the V-2, the Viking sounding rocket was successful, but ultimately cancelled due to high costs. It was revived to create the first stage of the Vanguard launch vehicle, with the XLR10 modified to create the XLR50 (X-405).

The Reaction Motors XLR11 (internal designation 6000C-4) was a small rocket motor designed to power experimental high-speed aircraft, including the X-1, early X-15s, X-24B, and D-558-2. Its four combustion chambers were ignited independently, which is represented as the ability to throttle in discrete steps.

The XLR25 was designed for the X-2, to test higher speeds and altitudes than the X-1. It was the first continuously throttleable engine designed in the US. Although the engine was successful, the X-2 proved extremely unstable at high speeds and only a few flights were undertaken.
A small rocket motor intended to be used on the XF8U-3 for increased performance. Cancelled after the prototype exploded during testing and the XF8U-3 was cancelled in favor of the F4H.
Americanized version of the V-2 Model 39 (A-4). It was very similar to its predecessor, but was built using American SAE components rather than metric components, and featured several minor upgrades.
A LOX/Ammonia gas generator engine which powered the X-15 spaceplane. It was the first large rocket engine capable of throttling and restarting.
Rocketdyne's pump-fed high performance upper stage engine for perigee/apogee stages, as well as transfer vehicles and lunar and Martian missions. It was tested extensively but has never flown.
A linear aerospike engine developed for NASA's X-33 sub-scale SSTO technology demonstrator. Like the toroidal J-2T engines, the XRS-2200 used machinery derived from the J-2S.

A Chinese hypergolic gas generator booster engine. Derived from the Isayev S2.1100 Burya booster engine, four YF-1 engines form the YF-2 booster used on the first stage of the DF-3, DF-4, and Long March 1 rockets.
A Chinese hypergolic gas generator vacuum engine. Derived from the Isayev S2.1100 Burya booster engine, the YF-3 is a vacuum variant created for the second stage of the DF-4 and Long March 1.

A Chinese hypergolic gas generator booster engine. Four YF-20 engines form the YF-21 booster used on the first stage of the DF-5, FB-1, and Long March 2/3/4 rockets, as well as the strap-on boosters for the Long March 2/3.
A Chinese hypergolic gas generator vacuum engine. A YF-22 engine and YF-23 vernier form the YF-24 engine unit used on the second stage of the DF-5, FB-1, and Long March 2/3/4 rockets.
A Chinese hypergolic gas generator vacuum engine with verniers. A YF-22 engine and YF-23 vernier form the YF-24 engine unit used on the second stage of the DF-5, FB-1, and Long March 2/3/4 rockets.
A Chinese hypergolic gas generator vacuum engine, created for the 3rd stage of the Long March 4. Later versions had restart capability.
The first operational Chinese hydrolox gas generator vacuum engine. Used on the third stage of the Long March 3. Low performance and unreliable, it was replaced by the YF-75 after 13 flights.

A Chinese hydrolox gas generator vacuum engine, created to replace the YF-73. Used on the third stage of the Long March 3A/B/C. It was converted to expander cycle to create the YF-75D, which is used on the second stage of Long March 5.
A Chinese hydrolox gas generator sustainer engine. Used on the first stage of the Long March 5.

A Chinese kerolox staged combustion booster engine. Based on the RD-120, it is the first staged combustion engine developed in China, and is used on the boosters of the Long March 5, as well as the boosters and first stage of the Long March 6, 7, and 8.

An early 1960s nuclear turbo-ramjet, designed for supersonic bombers. One of the ultimate direct-cycle designs produced by the Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion (ANP) program, the A-136 used a hybrid cycle to improve supersonic performance. By tapping off a small amount of air to cool the turbine, turbine inlet temperatures could be managed, while the remaining air passed straight through the reactor and was heated to full temperature. This gave the engine good performance up to Mach 3. It also included a kerosene burner to improve takeoff thrust.
An early 50s turbojet which served as the powerplant for the Su-7, Su-9, Su-11, Tu-128, and Be-10 flying boat.

The AL-31 is a early 1980s low-bypass turbofan, designed to power the Su-27. Despite difficult development, resulting in early Su-27s being equipped with the AL-21 engine, it ultimately proved successful, powering the Su-27, Su-30, Su-34, Su-35, Su-57, J-10 and J-11. Later models were also equipped with thrust vectoring capability. Modernized AL-31s were designated AL-41F-1, not to be confused with the AL-41, an unrelated design from the late 1980s.

The Atar 08/09 was a late-1950s redesign of the Atar 101, increasing thrust (creating the Atar 08) and adding an afterburner (creating the Atar 09). The Atar 09 powered the next generation of French jet aircraft, including the Cheetah C/D/E/R, Mirage III/IV, and Mirage F1.
The Atar 101 was one of the first jet engines developed in France following WW2. It was used in many early French jet aircraft, including the Vautour I/II, Gerfaut I, and Mystère II.

The Avon was Rolls-Royce's first axial-flow turbojet, introduced in 1950. It powered most British aircraft of the 1950s and 60s, including the Sea Vixen, Canberra, Lightning, Hunter, Swift and Valiant.

The CF6 high-bypass turbofan was developed from the TF39, the first ever production high-bypass turbofan. It powered many large aircraft, including the A300, A310, A330, B747, B767, DC-10, KC-10, MD-11, E-4, C-2, and C-5M.

The TF34 is a 1970s high-bypass turbofan. It powered the S-3, S-72, and A-10, while its civilian derivative, the CF34, powered many large private jets and regional airliners such as the Challenger 600 Series, Challenger 850, CRJ100/200/440/700/900, and the Embraer 170/175/190/195.

The CFM56 is a 1970s high-bypass turbofan, developed from the F101. Created in a collaboration between GE and Snecma, the CFM56 is the most successful high-bypass turbofan ever made, with over 30,000 built. It powered the Airbus A320 and A340 series, B737 Classic and Next Gen series, DC-8-70, and was used to re-engine many 707-based aircraft such as the E-3, E-6, and KC/RC-135.
The Chimera is a combined cycle ramjet tech demonstrator built by Hermeus. Based around retired J85 cores, it is intended to operate over a flight envelope from Mach 0 to Mach 5.
The D-18 was the largest high-bypass turbofan developed in the Soviet Union, created in the 1980s for the An-124 and An-225.

The D-30 is one of the first turbofan engines developed in the Soviet Union, and the most successful. While originally developed to power the Tu-134 airliner, it found its way into many Soviet aircraft, including the Tu-154, Il-62, Il-76, M-55, and with afterburner, MiG-31 and Su-47.

The Derwent was a development of the W.2 / Welland engine with "straight through flow" rather than "reverse flow," leading to an increase in thrust and efficiency. It was a short-lived line of engines, ending with World War II; indeed, the Derwent V was in fact a scaled-down Nene. Powered the Meteor F.3/F.4/NF.12/NF.14, Nord 1601, Sagittario II, and Yak-23/25/30 and La-15 as the license-built RD-500.
A large, 16 kW electric ducted fan. Very powerful for it's size, but fixed pitch propeller blades limit it to low speeds.
The EJ200 is a 1990s low-bypass turbofan, designed as a joint venture between many European companies for the Eurofighter Typhoon.

The F100 is a 1970s low-bypass turbofan designed for the F-15 and F-16. Its advanced design and high power allowed the F-15 and F-16 to achieve a thrust to weight ratio greater than one. It was used in all F-15 and most F-16 variants.

The F119 is a 1990s low-bypass turbofan designed for the Advance Tactical Fighter program. Designed for supercruise capability, it has unusually high dry thrust for its size, and it has a 2D thrust-vectoring nozzle for increased maneuverability. It was used in the F-22, YF-23, X-32 and X-35.

The F135 is a 2000s low-bypass turbofan designed for the F-35. Two variants exist, with a conventional nozzle for the F-35A/C, and one with a forward PTO shaft and gimbaled nozzle for the VTOL-capable F-35B.

The F404 is a 1970s low-bypass turbofan designed for the F/A-18. It was designed for reliability rather than performance, in order to replace the notoriously unreliable F-4s and F-14s used by the US Navy and Marines at the time. It was used in the F/A-18A/B/C/D, F-20A, F-117A, T-7A, T-50, JAS-39, and Tejas.

The GE4 was a 1970s turbojet developed to power the Boeing 2707 supersonic transport at speeds up to Mach 2.7. The most powerful turbojet ever made, the GE4 was tested extensively, but ultimately cancelled with the rest of the 2707 project.
The GEnx is a 2000s large, high-bypass turbofan, developed from the GE90 to power the B787. It is used in most 787 variants, as well as in the 747-8.

The Allison/General Electric J35 is an axial flow turbojet, and one of the first turbojets natively designed in the United States. Although not as well known as its later derivative, the J47, it still powered many late 40s aircraft such as the FJ-1, F-84, F-89, XP-86, XB-45, XB-47, X-5, and D-558.
An early 1950s turbojet, developed from the earlier J35 by General Electric. It powered the F-86, FJ-2, B-36, B-45, and B-48.

The J48 was also known as the Rolls-Royce Tay. Essentially an enlarged Nene, it was abandoned by Rolls-Royce in favor of the Avon. However, Pratt & Whitney was able to acquire the design, and produced it as the J48. It was used in the F9F-5 Panther, F9F-6/8 Cougar, F-94C Starfire, and YF-93.
The J57 was a workhorse, designed in the early 1950s and powering the B-52, most of the Century Series fighters, and even the U-2.
Designed in the late 1950s, the J58 was redesigned and repurposed for one use: Mach 3+ aircraft like the A-12 / SR-71A/B / YF-12A. Also known by it's civilian designation, JT11.
Essentially a larger J57, the P&W J75 saw extensive military and civilian use. It was used on the F-105, F-106, F-107, XF8U-3, A-12, U-2, P6M, and the 707 and DC-8 as the JT4A.
The first US "Mach 2" engine, the J79 saw extensive service, powering the B-58, F-4, A-5, and F-104.

The J85 was developed as a small, disposable jet engine to power decoys and drones, but was later upgraded for use on manned aircraft. It powered many small aircraft, including the F-5, CF-5, G.91Y, T-2, T-38, and A-37.
Derived from the J79, the J93 was developed for Mach 3 performance to power the B-70 and F-108.

Derived from the J52, the JT8D was an early low-bypass turbofan, used on many second-generation jetliners like the Boeing 727, 737, and DC-9. It received a substantial redesign in the 1970s, creating the JT8D-200 series, which powered the Super 27, MD-80 series, and was used to upgrade many 707-based aircraft like the E-8C.

A late 50s turbojet based on the Pratt & Whitney J57, the Model 304-2 was a liquid-hydrogen-fueled turbojet, designed for project SUNTAN, a high-performance replacement for the U-2 spyplane. The project required the development of large-scale liquid hydrogen production and handling techniques, at the cost of hundreds of millions of dollars. Various jet engines were converted to hydrogen power, where they showed incredible stability and efficiency. This information, along with many of the engineers involved, were later transferred to working on the RL-10 where the information gained proved invaluable. The Model 304 and project SUNTAN, however, were ultimately cancelled, as the conventionally-fueled A-12/SR-71 was showing much greater promise.

The NK-8 was a 1960s low-bypass turbofan, created to power the Il-62 and Tu-154. It was later modified for improved performance to power the Il-86, and modified to run on alternate fuels for the Tu-155 project. It powered the A-90, Il-62, Il-62M, Tu-154, Tu-154A/B and Tu-155.
The NK-12 was a large 1950s turboprop. Created to power the Tu-95, it is the largest turboprop to enter production. It powered the A-90, An-22, Tu-95, Tu-114, Tu-116, Tu-126, and Tu-142.

The NK-144 was a 1960s low-bypass turbofan developed from the NK-8 to power the Tu-144 supersonic transport. The NK-144 was unable to meet performance requirements and was replaced by the RD-36, but found new life as the NK-22, which powered the Tu-22M0/M1/M2.
The NK-25 was a 1970s low-bypass turbofan, developed from the earlier NK-22. It is the most powerful supersonic jet engine ever flown, and was used to power the Tu-22M3, Tu-160, Tu-160M and Tu-144LL.

The Nord 1500 ramjet was a combined cycle ramjet, mated to an Atar 101E. Used on the Griffon II experimental aircraft, the Atar 101 would accelerate the aircraft up to the speed of sound, at which point the ramjet could act as a thrust augmentor and accelerate aircraft up to speeds over Mach 2. Although the Griffon II performed well, it was cancelled in favor of more conventional aircraft.

A late 1960s turbojet. The ultimate version of the Olympus turbojet, designed for sustained Mach 2 operation to power Concorde. Although thirsty at sea level, when mated to a well-optimized intake this engine can supercruise at Mach 2, achieving relatively good efficiency.

An early 1960s small turboprop. Developed for midsize general aviation aircraft, the PT6A was first used on the Beechcraft King Air. It's low cost, low weight, and high reliability led to it becoming one of the most popular turboprop engines ever, with over 60,000 built. It is offered in many large general aviation and small commercial aircraft, and is popular as an upgrade to older piston-engined aircraft.

A late 50s turbojet, the R-11 was developed in parallel with the less sophisticated RD-9. It became the powerplant for the MiG-21, Yak-28 and Su-15. It was reverse-engineered in China and built as the WP-7, where it powered the JJ-7, J/F-7, and J-8.

A late 60s turbojet, the R-13 was developed from the earlier R-11 to improve the performance of the MiG-21. It became the powerplant for late model MiG-21s and Su-15s. It was reverse-engineered in China and built as the WP-13, where it powered the J-7III onwards and J-8II.

A late 50s turbojet originally developed for the Tu-121 cruise missile, the R-15 was modified instead for use on the MiG-25, which became the fastest serially produced fighter, capable of reaching Mach 3.2, although at the risk of severe engine damage.
A late 60s turbojet. Developed to replace the R-11 and R-13, the R-25 added an extremely powerful "extra-power" afterburner, that allowed it to nearly double it's thrust for short periods of time.

A 1980s afterburning turbofan, designed for the Yak-41. It was equipped with an engine gimbal system that allowed the nozzle to rotate 95 degrees, to support vertical flight, and was the first engine of this type equipped with an afterburner, allowing the Yak-41 to achieve supersonic flight. It powered the Yak-141/41, and was proposed to power the Su-47 with the thrust vectoring system removed.

The RB.162 was a lightweight turbojet, designed to be used as a liftjet for VTOL aircraft. It utilized fiberglass and plastic extensively in it's construction to reduce weight as much as possible, resulting in a low lifetime but very high thrust-to-weight ratio. It was used as a liftjet on the Do-31, Mirage IIIV, and VAK 191B, and as a booster engine on the Trident 3B to improve takeoff performance.

An early 50s turbojet. Developed as a scaled down Mikulin AM-3, the RD-9 was designed for fighter aircraft and powered the Yak-25, 26, 27, 28, and MiG-19. It was license-built in China as the WP-6, where it powered the JJ-6, J/F-6, Q/A-5, and J-12.

The RD-36 was a 1970s turbojet, developed to power the Tu-144. The RD-36 replaced the underperforming NK-144 engines, allowing the Tu-144 to achieve its intended range. Ultimately, the Tu-144 was taken out of service shortly after being upgraded due to costs. The RD-36 powered the Tu-144D and M-17.

The RD-41 was a lightweight turbojet, designed as an improved version of the RD-36 liftjet for the Yak-141/41M. It was provided with a gimballing engine mount, allowing for 12.5 degrees of deflection to improve stability while hovering. Used as the liftjet on the Yak-141/41M.
The RD-012 was a supersonic ramjet, designed to power the La-350 Burya cruise missile up to Mach 3.1.

The RJ43 was a supersonic ramjet, designed to power the CIM-10 Bomarc surface to air missile at speeds up to Mach 3. It was also used on the X-7 and XQ-5/AQM-60 target drone, and was modified to power the D-21 up to speeds over Mach 3.3.
The RJ47 was a supersonic ramjet, designed to power the SM-64 Navaho cruise missile up to Mach 2.75.

The RJ55 was a combined cycle ramjet, mated to a J67. At low speeds, the RJ55 functioned as an afterburner for the J67 turbojet, but at mach 2.24 the turbojet would be shut down and the RJ55 would power the aircraft up to Mach 3. Designed for the XF-103, but difficuties with the J67 turbojet meant the prototype never flew under it's own power.

The RJ59 was a supersonic ramjet, designed to power the Convair Super Hustler. Although the Super Hustler was cancelled, the RJ59 was fitted to the X-7 for testing, where it was able to achieve speeds over Mach 4.
An early 1950s turbojet. Derived from the MetroVick F.2, the first axial-flow jet developed in Britain, the Sapphire powered the Hawker Hunter, Handley Page Victor, and Gloster Javelin.
A Soviet-built derivative of the Nene used in many early Soviet jet aircraft, including the MiG-15, MiG-17, Tu-14, and Il-28.
The Welland was an early 1940s turbojet, developed from Frank Whittle's original jet engine, the W.1. It was used on the Meteor F.1, but was quickly replaced by later, more powerful jet engines.

The WS-10 is a modern low-bypass afterburning turbofan, and the first successful Chinese turbofan design. Developed from the earlier experimental WS-6 turbofan, the WS-10 was designed to replace the Russian AL-31 engines used in some Chinese aircraft. The WS-10 powers the J-8II, J-10B/C, J-11B, J-15, J-16, and J-20/A.

The Atar 101 was one of the first jet engines developed in France following WW2. It was used in many early French jet aircraft, including the Vautour I/II, Gerfaut I, and Mystère II. This is the 101D, an early model used in the Dassault Mystère IIC. Available 1954. Thrust 29.42kN. OPR 4.5, SFC 1.09 lb/lbf-hr static. Temperature limit Mach 1.5.

The Derwent V, rather than being a development of the Derwent line (a straight-through-flow development of the W.2), was instead a scaled-down Nene. It powered the Meteor F.4, and also the La-15, Yak-23 and Yak-25 as the RD-500, a Soviet-built copy. Thrust 15.6kN. Available in mid-late 1945. OPR 4.0, SFC 1.03 lb/lbf-hr static. Temperature limit Mach 1.

The Allison/General Electric J35 is an axial flow turbojet, and one of the first turbojets natively designed in the United States. Although not as well known as it's later derivative, the J47, it still powered many late 40s aircraft such as the FJ-1, F-84, F-89, XP-86, XB-45, XB-47, X-5, and D-558. This is the -11, as used on the Douglas D-558-1. Available 1946. Thrust 16.68kN. 4.0 OPR, SFC of 1.12lb/lbf-hr static. Temperature limit Mach 1.

The General Electric J47 is an axial flow turbojet, developed from the J35 in parallel with centrifugal flow jets based on British designs. The J47 was very successful, used on many early 50s aircraft, including the F-86, FJ-2, XF-87, XF-91, B-36, B-45, B-47, XB-51, KB-50, KB-97, and even the M-497 jet-powered railcar. This is the -27, a later model used in the F-86F. Available 1952. Thrust 26.47 kN. 5.5 OPR, SFC of 0.902lb/lbf-hr static. Temperature limit Mach 1.

A Soviet-built derivative of the Nene. The British government sold several Nene and Derwent engines to the Soviet Union in 1946, which were then reverse engineered, and used in many early Soviet jet aircraft, including the MiG-15, MiG-17, and Il-28. The VK-1 was an improved version, used in the MiG-15bis. Available 1949. Thrust 26.47 kN. 4.4 OPR, SFC 1.049 lb/lbf-hr static. Temperature limit Mach 1.

Androgynous Peripheral Attach System developed for the Shuttle-Mir program and ISS. This is the active variant, with a deployable capture ring to align the ports and dampen the impact.

Androgynous Peripheral Attach System developed for the Shuttle-Mir program and ISS. This is the passive variant, useful for permanent fixtures that won't have to form the active docking partner, such as berthing ports on station modules.
The attitude control thruster blocks of the Apollo Service Module (SM). Four of these allow full three-axis attitude control and translation of the Apollo CSM.
The Command Module of the Apollo spacecraft. Apollo was the spacecraft that transported humans to the Moon in the 1960's and 1970's. It has room for three crew.
This is used to decouple the Command Module from the Service Module prior to reentry.
Docking spotlight to provide illumination for docking/berthing operations. Attach to the Apollo Service Module decoupler.
This is the drogue (accepting) part of the Apollo Docking System. It will only work with the Apollo Command Module Probe.
Apollo Command Module Drogue Parachute Pack

The drogue parachute pack is meant to slow down the Apollo spacecraft at a high altitude in preparation for the deployment of the main parachute pack. Attach this to the front node before placing the Forward Heat Shield.
The engine mount for the Apollo SM contains mounting points for the Apollo SPS, HGA, and other accessories.
EVA spotlight to provide illumination for EVA operations. Attach to the Apollo Service Module decoupler.
Apollo Command Module Forward Heat Shield
The forward heat shield for the Apollo Command Module. Attach this to the top of the CM after placing the Drogue and Main Parachutes.
The primary High Gain Antenna of the Apollo Spacecraft. Attach to the node on the Service Module Engine Mount.
Lunar-rated heatshield for the Apollo Capsule.

The abort motor of the LES is a powerful solid rocket motor, designed specifically to carry away the Apollo Command Module in the case of a pad or a low altitude flight abort. The pitch motor of the LES imparts a small attitude change to the Apollo Command Module during an abort. This ensures that the CM will have sufficient clearance from the launch vehicle after the LES abort motor burns out. The first engine module is the Escape Motor, the second module is the Jettison Motor, and the third is the pitch motor. Fire the escape and pitch motors to abort, then activate the jettision motor to pull the tower clear of the CM.
Aerodynamic nosecone used on Apollo Block I, since docking missions weren't planned until Block II.
Apollo Command Module Main Parachute Pack
The main parachute pack of the Apollo Command Module. Attach this to the front node before placing the Forward Heat Shield.
This is the probe part of the Apollo Docking System. It will only work with the Apollo Docking Mechanism Drogue.
VHF scimitar antenna to provide ship-to-ship comms and act as a backup for the main high-gain antenna. Place two on opposite sides of the SM and LM.
The Apollo Service Module contains the main propellant tanks, the fuel cells, life support and everything else that it is needed for a flight to the Moon.
An extending dipole antenna used to gather high frequency radar sounding data. Can be used as a communications antenna in a pinch. Attach in a pair to the nodes on the Apollo engine plate.

A folding Yagi antenna designed to enhance gathering of VHF radar sounding data. Can be used as a communications antenna in a pinch. Attach to the node on the Apollo engine mount just under the science bay.
Apollo Block IV CADS Active Docking Port

Common Androgynous Docking Port. Developed to eliminate the limitations of the gendered Apollo docking system, as well as provide a larger passageway for delivering cargo. Equipped with a deployable capture ring to dampen impact. Permanent station ports can use the passive version, which is simpler and lighter.

LEO Heatshield for the Apollo Block III+ Capsule. A lighter heat shield for use with LEO operations.

In order to increase the living space and mission duration of the Apollo Block III CSM. This mission module is essentially several more cubic meters of living space for the crew. Place it upside down in place of the lunar module, with docking ports on each end. Extract with the CSM after circularization. FICTIONAL (Eyes Turned Skyward)

Following the introduction of more capable lifters for crewed LEO missions, the venerable Apollo Block III+ mission module was replaced with a larger can. Includes a larger attachment node on top for using larger androgynous docking ports. Place it upside down in place of the lunar module, with docking ports on each end. Extract with the CSM after circularization.

The ascent stage and crew compartment of the Apollo Lunar Module.
The explosive bolt interstage connector placed between the ascent and the descent modules of the Apollo Lunar Module.

Apollo LM Material Experiment Stowage Assembly
Storage bay, containing astronaut EVA equipment, and cameras to record the first steps onto the moon. Place to the left of the LM ladder.

The LM Taxi Ascent Stage Cockpit provides accommodations for up to three crew to ride to the Moon's surface atop the LM Decent Stage, perform an extended surface stay, then return to orbit. During surface operations, the Taxi is shut down and put in a dormant state to save resources, while the crew operates out of a separately landed shelter. Includes radiators and deployable insulation for the dormancy period. Remember to have all crew members on board before launching. Due to low performance with 3 crewmembers, it is recommended to leave behind all equipment before launching.
Folding SNAP-27 mount. Used for upgraded lunar missions that need to have keep-alive power and heat during the dormancy period of a long sortie.
Radial quad-mount version of the SNAP-9 RTG. Used for upgraded lunar missions that need to have keep-alive power and heat during the dormancy period of a long sortie.

Longer surface stays require facilities and consumables beyond what can be carried in a single LM lander. This is a dedicated shelter module. Includes fuel cells, deployable insulation, and an expandable airlock - make sure your front leg does not have the "porch". Requires additional oxygen tanks to be added to the descent module to supply the crew and fuel cells.
This platform is intended to be mounted on top of a LM Descent Stage. Includes extending ramps for deploying a rover to the lunar surface. Rover design or parts not included.

Androgynous Peripheral Attachment System 75. First fully androgynous docking port, designed for the Apollo Soyuz Test Project.

A specialized module designed to allow the docking of two separate spacecraft to either end of this module. In addition to mating spacecraft, it provides additional living/working space, as well as a platform for experiments.
Apollo-Soyuz Test Project UV Absorbtion Experiment

This experiment is a modified and slightly enhanced version of the Far Ultraviolet Spectrometer. This experiment can be used to study measure emissions from celestial bodies, zodiacal light, solar atmosphere emissions, stellar emissions, and galactic emissions.
A small, fixed VHF-FM whip antenna for the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project Docking Module.
A small extending antenna used for maintaining communications between the Gemini spacecraft and the ground. Attaches to the equipment section
The Gemini cabin. Contains two astronauts. When equipped with fuel cells and combined with its service module, it is capable of complex, long duration space missions.

The Gemini Adapter Equipment Section. It contains O2 and H2 for fuel cell consumption and life support. It also contains fuel for manoeuvring and attitude control thrusters. This is the configuration as found on Gemini 10+. RCS O/F Ratio 1.223:1.
Heatshield for the Gemini Capsule, capable of lifting LEO reentry. Can be switched to the Gemini B configuration with a hatch.

Improved, lunar rated heatshield for the Gemini Capsule. Can be switched to the Gemini B configuration with a hatch. Gemini lacks the radiative heat protection of more advanced capsules. Extremely gentle Lunar reentries only.
Gemini L was one proposal for an advanced Gemini pod capable of reentry from translunar trajectory. This would have included development of an improved TPS similar to the system used on Apollo.
Covers up the nose of the Gemini Docking Mechanism to protect it during ascent. Jettison once out of the atmosphere.

One of the most crucial skills that the Gemini program is meant to develop is the ability to rendezvous and dock in space. This simple docking mechanism doesn't have the ability to transfer crew or resources, but it will allow you to connect two vessels in flight. This male active docking mechanism corresponds to the female Agena Docking Adapter. It include an indexing key, that slides into the V shape on the Agena Docking Adapter, to help line the two craft up properly.
A lighter nosecone for Gemini without the docking port.

This tiny thruster is nevertheless more than sufficient to manuever the Gemini capsule around in low orbit. This part is configured as RCS.

Main parachute for Gemini. Attaches on top of the Gemini Re-entry Control System.

Gemini retro solid derived from the Star 13 orbit insertion motor. Place in 4x symmetry in the gaps of the retro module cruciform.
Low profile decoupler for separating the Gemini capsule from the Adapter Retrograde Section.
This hollow structural adapter is designed to sit on top of the Gemini equipment section and house a quad of retro motors for reentry. Houses six translational control thrusters.

As operations in space become more complex, more crew members are needed. This expanded crew module replaces the standard Gemini service module, allowing seven additional crew members to ride to space. To be used with either a modified Apollo Service Module for deep space operations, or the Big Gemini Service Module for LEO operations.
This decoupler is designed to sit between a capsule's heatshield, and the service module. It includes an umbilical to connect the capsule to the service module's systems.
Structural docking adapter for Big Gemini. Ideally sized for the Apollo active docking port.
Heatshield for the Big Gemini capsule
Lunar heatshield for the Big Gemini capsule. Gemini lacks the radiative heat protection of more advanced capsules. Extremely gentle Lunar reentries only.

This solid rocket tower is designed to wrench the command pod up and away from a malfunctioning rocket. Use only in case of emergency. WARNING: Staging the LES will also decouple it from the bottom node, in order to dispose of it after launch. Map the engine to the ABORT action group for emergency use.
This large docking module is used to connect MOL segments to each other. It is capable of soft docking to line up the segments, before retracting and solidifying the connection.
This is an enlarged Gemini nose fairing to allow the installation of larger parachutes for Big Gemini. All rendezvous and docking equipment has been removed to save weight.
Enlarged main parachute for Big Gemini. Attaches on top of the Gemini Re-entry Control System.
Enlarged drogue parachute for the Big Gemini. Attach to the node in the nose section.

A large 2.5m+ service module for the 1969 Big Gemini concept. Includes a large pressurized volume in the aft for cargo and crew space. This Service Module is also compatible with Apollo (although it will need a custom adapter, and the internal compartment will be inaccessable since Apollo doesn't have a hatch in it's heat shield), and the Apollo Service Module is also compatible with Big Gemini (Adapter not included). NOTE: This contains no propulsion, add RCS thrusters.

Upon being bribed for further information, the participants revealed that xenon-powered ion engines were the current trending item. When the excursion is over, it serves as the launch pad for the ascent stage. It also carries a Surface Experiment Package and has some room for KIS storage.

The Ascent stage houses the crew cabin with instrument panels and flight controls. It contains its own Ascent Propulsion System (APS) engine and propellant tanks for return to munar orbit and rendezvous with the Command/Service Module. It also contains a Reaction Control System (RCS) for attitude and translation control. A forward EVA hatch provides access to and from the munar surface, while an overhead docking port provides access to and from the Command Module.

A long time ago a Kerbal said “Give me a place to stand and with a lever I will move the whole world” - while he turned out to be frothing mad, the principle still applies. STEADLER have mounted a RV-105 RCS block on a boom to provide a larger moment for rotation.
Probodobodyne Inc's first and only foray into crew habitation modules. Bulky, but not uncomfortable. It even features a handy set of exterior handrails.

Slows you down. Well, providing you're in an atmosphere. It won't help on the Mun, unlike parachutes which definitely work there. Honest guv. Also doubles as a handy surfboard.

The airlock was designed shortly after the term 'Explosive Decompression' was coined. It allows Kerbals to move from the interior of the vessel to the exterior without a great change in internal pressure.

Pip pip, old boy! Light, cheap and packing a not inconsiderable punch, the Black Adder-8 certainly offers 'bang for buck', as the chaps over at the KSC say. Perfect for a budding space program, although quickly outclassed by more high-tech engines.

Built with spares from the BA-8. Well, we had to do something, they really were just cluttering the place up. Does make it cheaper than pesky Rockomax's 48-7S. And we have two nozzles, more is always better.

Built with completely peaceful motives, nothing else. Features a rear seat to allow for a scientist or engineer to accompany the pilot and a top of the range 'hole in the floor'. That's for taking pretty pictures, not aiming anything explosive. Honest.

Kerlington's companion to the Bonny. The Clyde allows for easy transport of a '3 piece' crew by a pilot, either between facilities or from landing locations.

Through exploitation of the natural decay of Blutonium-238, this elegantly simple power generator can provide consistent, stable power for decades. Comes in a lovely waterproof container.

A top of the line habitat meant for long-term operations. Typically after the initial 'colonists' made their situation more 'permanent' with a bit of lithobreaking. Features cabins, food preparation areas, sofas, space loos, and even a home gym.

Less 'high tech spaceship part', more 'we spent the budget on food and this was the only thing we could find lying around'. The designers did manage to add a smaller sub-tank for oxidiser, although the words 'plastic bag - Oxidiser goes here' can be seen on the blueprints.
An uncharacteristic foray into airliner control systems from Probodobodyne, the Goose provides a reliable avionics base and a 3 person crew for longer range flights and extra nap time.
Mounted with batteries for extended operations, a set of more powerful reaction wheels and some modest truss work, the HECS-Ranger is an excellent choice for the larger, more reserved probe.
Vac-Co's answer to C7 Aerospace's Circular Turboprop intake. Slightly less efficient, but slightly lighter. Plus it has a spinny-round bit.

The KDB's contender for a 2.5m orbital rocket engine. While less powerful that Rockomax's "Poodle", its lower profile and strengthened casing does make it easier to land on if you happen to forget your landing legs.

The L.A.N.C.E.R. is the result of the continuing joint venture between C7 Aerospace and the Rockomax Conglomerate. Designed to fill a gap in the design requirements for large, sustainable single-stage-to-orbit aircraft, this engine combines the best of rocket and air-breathing thrust technology.

While similar to the Mk2 Lander Can internally, it offers a ruggedised casing and better crash resistance, plus handy EVA handgrips (pun intended). However, smaller and less powerful reaction wheels had to be mounted to compensate.

The TT06-A Stability Enhancer uses ground-breaking fastening technology to significantly increase the stability of spacecraft during the pre-launch phase. While OMB Demolition has been criticized in the past for using "big fancy words for a rocket holder" in their description of their device, none can say the TT18 series doesn't deliver rock-solid clamping action, as advertised. The owner's manual strongly suggests these devices be placed on the bottommost section of the spacecraft, and activated as soon as the engines are lit, for optimal de-clamping performance.
The counter proposal to the LV-T45 from the 'Bigger is always better' side of the R&D department. More powerful, but lacking the control authority of its smaller cousin.

The EAS 316 is a lightweight observation pod that works in the same way as the EAS-1 External Command Seat. Features a 'No key' start button, though that just means that the pilots have normally gone back to the KSC to find the non-existent keys on launch.

lander orbit propuls rocket (beagle vacuum sustain (ven (vsr
The largest monopropellant tank available. It's actually made of four smaller tanks, but we won't tell if you won't.
fueltank mono monopropellant propellant ven vsr

Pratt & Whitney Double Wasp, 2250HP (2650HP wet). Water-injected radial with a strong three-speed (only 2 modeled) two-stage supercharger. Note, due to modeling issues, will only develop rated altitude horsepower when at maximum speed. Used on P-61B Black Widow.
1640 at 2500rpm at takeoff, 1450hp at 2400rpm at 4650m, 750hp at 10500m. Two-speed single-stage supercharger.
Wright Twin Cyclone, 1600HP radial. Two-speed supercharger. 1450HP at 4.7km static. 11ft 3in 3-blade constant-speed propeller.

Wright Twin Cyclone, 1600HP radial. Two-speed turbosupercharger. Maintains just under 1400HP until about 6km. Turbocharger adds considerable weight, complexity, and size, however. 11ft 3in 3-blade constant-speed propeller.
Pratt & Whitney Twin Wasp, 1350HP radial. Two-speed supercharger, max of 1395HP at 3km and 1365HP at 5km static, 1415/3.6 and 1387/5.6 with ram air.
An adjustable landing gear with two wheels and slightly stronger brakes, motor, and default suspension settings.
An adjustable landing gear with a single wheel.
When trying to prank Valentina, Jeb filled the engine of her private jet with iron filings. The result was an engine the produces no thrust, but plenty of electricity.

Repurposed from the construction equipment that was used to originally build the KSC, this general purpose industrial hydraulic leg can fill a wide range of uses when clearance and stability are needed.
"Low velocity anti-lithbraking devices". Gene Kerman just calls them repulsors. Gimbal, steering, propulsion, and brakes not included.
KF Anti Grav motor - Surface mount
A slimline surface mount repulsor. Not as stable as their bigger cousins, though just as capable and pocket sized. Though biscuit shaped, they are NOT SNACKS!
Dubbed the HypnoDrive by those fortunate enough to use it and survive its hypnotic charms, this alternate mode of amphibious propulsion comes in handy when wheels are just plain.... boring!
Fed up with those pesky hypnotic rotating things mesmerising Kerbals and causing accidents, kebal engineers decided to make something a little less.... hypnotic. We leave the results up to you.
The crate simply says: "Please fit the right way up. Enjoy any which way." Ironically, it has no "this way up" sticker. Warranty void if inverted.
Long and powerful track. It's suited to support heavy panzer look-alikes but can be used for more civilized duties. Like flipping over on slopes.

Originally a treadmill for sharpening up lazy interns, this track unit soon fell into widespread use when a bored engineer flipped it over, strapped a battery pack to it, and set it running out of the SPH, shouting "BE FREE!"

After Jeb returned from a failed snack run caused by a mysterious red spacecraft, the kerbals were left with some rather large track units which fell out of a strange green hypersonic craft that flew over shortly after...

Inspired by his favourite childhood series "Thunder Kats", Gene Kerman was inspired to created this oddly shaped track unit. Useful for smaller craft, as well as remote control snack delivery units. Snacks not included.

Flying in the face of the usual "Go big or go home" philosophy, junior Kerbal engineer Dougel Kerman came up with these after looking at a larger prototype 'from far away'. Valentina thinks they're cute.
When messing with some old shopping trolley wheels and large rubber bands left by the postman after a delivery or rocket parts, Bill came up with this handy wheel/track thing.
A very small track unit. Bed springs were used.

Optimised for Kerbin straight out of its wooden crate - though tweakable for higher gravity - this wheel is designed for large, high-mobility planetary rovers. Criticised for being power-hungry, but never for being over powered! (Warning: Extremely over powered. Warranty void when used under the influence of gravity.)
Mid size wheels for serious rovers. Good suspension travel and rugged designs make these ideal for serious roving and snack runs..
A tiny set of wheel for autonomous rovers
A small but rugged wheel that can fill a wide variety of roles. The dual wheels increase load capacity compared to the single-wheel model, as well as being equipped with a higher capacity motor.
A small but rugged wheel that can fill a wide variety of roles.
An even larger version of the chemical plant, for housing base-scale ISRU processes.
A larger version of the chemical plant, for housing ISRU processes.
A large part for turning gaseous fuel or oxygen into liquid to be used.
A small part for turning gaseous fuel or oxygen into liquid to be used.

Thanks to advancements in virtual reality, digital entertainment and human health and psychology studies, permanent habitation is now possible. Some form of gravity is still required, so being landed or using a centrifuge is a necessity.
When Kerbals dream of space their first thought is often of Kerbal Space Center, the de facto home of spaceflight for the peoples of Kerbin.
Modular Launch Pads Launch Stand parts.
Modular Launch Pads Launch Plate parts.
Modular Launch Pads General Launch Base parts.
Modular Launch Pads Soyuz Launch Base parts.
Modular Launch Pads Saturn Mobile Launcher parts.
Modular Launch Pads Space Shuttle launcher parts.

Multi-configurable twin-arm umbilical that retracts in a folding motion, styled after the one used for the Ariane V rocket. Deploy limit sliders are used to adjust the arm spread, inner and outer arm lengths, and the rotation of the arms. The arms havr 8 color options, and each of the arm pipes have 5 color options. The umbilical retraction can be done manually or by staging.
Crew Access Arm Large - Large Mount

The Large General Crew Access Arm with a mount sized for the Large General Crew Elevator, with three style variants. The arm can be retracted either to the right (default) or left (alternate) by toggling the swing direction button. There are 6 arm length variants, and the end section can be adjusted inward up to 2.5m with the deploy limit slider. The end section also has 3 types of pod hatch interfaces. There is also an optional "transfer airlock" that can be boarded and used to transfer crew to a spacecraft inside a fairing.
Crew Access Arm Large - Small Mount

The Large General Crew Access Arm with a mount sized for the Small General Crew Elevator, with three style variants. The arm can be retracted either to the right (default) or left (alternate) by toggling the swing direction button. There are 3 arm length variants, and the end section can be adjusted inward up to 2.5m with the deploy limit slider. The end section also has 3 types of pod hatch interfaces. There is also an optional "transfer airlock" that can be boarded and used to transfer crew to a spacecraft inside a fairing.
Crew Access Arm Small - Mini Mount

The Small General Crew Access Arm with a mount for the Mini General Crew Elevator, available in 8 colors. Has 4 length variants, each with end or side hatch access styles. The end hatch access section can be adjusted inward using the deploy limit slider.
Crew Access Arm Small - Small Mount

The Small General Crew Access Arm with a mount for the Small General Crew Elevator, available in 8 colors. Has 5 length variants, each with end or side hatch access styles. The end hatch access section can be adjusted inward using the deploy limit slider.
Crew Elevator Large Base - 70m with Hatch

The base section for the Large General Crew Elevator tower with a 70m high elevator car. The separate elevator tower sections are attached to to the top. The base section has 8 color options and two toggleable styles of truss: General and Saturn types. Optional side panels in either 3 or 4-side configurations are also available. The elevator car's stopping height can be moved downward with the deploy limit slider. The elevator car can also be turned off. Hatch on the elevator car allows an alternate method of travel.

A side-mount walkway extension section for the Large General Crew Elevator. It attaches to one of the center nodes on the front of a tower section, or onto the tower section's optional side nodes, or onto the top of a tower section. The top floor is accessible, and there are optional middle and bottom floors as well. The four walls can be independently switched off to creat different walkway types. The wall trusses have two switchable styles: General and Saturn types. Optional bottom brace beams can also be separately switched on. There are also 8 color options.

A multi-height section for the Large General Crew Elevator tower, switchable between regular tower core and crew-access types. The section has 8 color options and two toggleable styles of truss: General and Saturn types. Optional side panels in multiple configurations are also available. The side pipes can also be turned off in different ways for use with the Extra Large General Crew Elevator.
The top plate for the Large General Crew Elevator tower. The railings and an antenna mast can be toggled on or off.
Crew Elevator Mini Core with Hatch

The Core section of the Mini General Crew Elevator tower for use with all launch bases, with a 32.0m high elevator car. The core has three height options; add additional Mini Crew Elevator Tower Sections to increase the core's height. The front wall can be partial on, full on or off. Uses the Small General Crew Arm - Mini mount, the Mercury-Atlas Crew Walkway or the Mini Crew Walkway for crew access to a spacecraft. Also has 8 color options. Adjust the height of the elevator car downward with the deploy limit slider to match the height of the crew arm or walkway and to use with the Tier 1 launch pad. Hatch on the elevator car allows an alternate method of travel.

Extra multi-height section for the Mini General Crew Elevator tower. Uses the Small General Crew Arm - Mini mount, the Mercury-Atlas Crew Walkway or the Mini Crew Walkway for crew access to a spacecraft. Also has 8 color options.
Crew Elevator Small Base with Hatch

The base section for the Small General Crew Elevator tower with a 50m high elevator car. The separate elevator tower sections are attached to to the top. The base section has 8 color options, and the front wall can be either partially turned off (leaving the horizontal beam), or fully removed, allowing a short elevator to be made for ground access to the deck of a launch base. The elevator car's stopping height can be moved downward with the deploy limit slider. The elevator car can also be turned off. Hatch on the elevator car allows an alternate method of travel.
A multi-height section for the Small General Crew Elevator tower, switchable between regular tower core and crew-access types. The section also has 8 color options.

The top plate for the Small General Crew Elevator tower. There are two styles of the plate, a full-size one and a U-shaped one. The railings and an antenna mast (different for each style of plate) can be toggled on or off.
Crew Elevator Extra Large Base - 130m with Hatch

The base section for the Extra Large General Crew Elevator tower with a 130m high elevator car. The separate elevator tower sections are attached to to the top. The base section has 8 color options and optional side panels in multiple configurations; the panel color can also be changed. The elevator car's stopping height can be moved downward with the deploy limit slider. The elevator car can also be turned off. Hatch on the elevator car allows an alternate method of travel.

A multi-height section for the Extra Large General Crew Elevator tower, switchable between regular tower core and crew-access types. The section has 8 color options and two toggleable styles of truss: General and Saturn types. Optional side panels in either 3 or 4-side configurations are also available.
Delta IV Swing Arm 1 - Core Tanks

Specialized animated swing arm for the Delta IV rocket. This is the lowest arm, which provides umbilicals for the core tanks. The arm's length and spread of the outer umbilical rails can be adjusted with the deploy limit sliders. The length of the umbilicals can also be separately adjusted, and the truss block spacers can be turned off as well, or the whole umbilical assembly can be turned off completely. The arm has 8 color options, and the two sets of arm pipes can be separately switched among 4 colors. Arm retraction is in only one direction.

Specialized animated swing arm for the Delta IV rocket. This is the middle arm, which provides umbilicals for the DCSS upper stage. The arm's length can be adjusted with the deploy limit slider. The length of the umbilical can also be adjusted. The arm has 8 color options, and the two sets of arm pipes can be separately switched among 4 colors. Arm retraction is in only one direction.

Specialized animated swing arm for the Delta IV rocket. This is the upper arm, which provides umbilicals for the fairing. The arm's length and vertical angle can be adjusted with the deploy limit sliders. The length of the umbilical can also be adjusted. The arm has 8 color options, and the two sets of arm pipes can be separately switched among 5 colors. Arm retraction is in only one direction.

A slimline general-use launch clamp, in between the integrated launch stands and the larger general launch bases. This is the medium frame type, and has multiple sizes of both square and rectangular exhaust holes. Uses separate towers and hold-downs. Built-in ladders can be switched both in height (short or tall) or color (default or yellow).

A slimline general-use launch clamp platform, in between the integrated launch stands and the larger general launch bases. This is the mini frame type, and has multiple sizes of both square and rectangular exhaust holes. Uses separate towers and hold-downs. Built-in ladders can be switched both in height (short or tall) or color (default or yellow).

A slimline general-use launch clamp platform, in between the integrated launch stands and the larger general launch bases. This is the small frame type, and has multiple sizes of both square and rectangular exhaust holes. Uses separate towers and hold-downs. Built-in ladders can be switched both in height (short or tall) or color (default or yellow).

Animated general-use truss-type fallback tower with multiple height variants and three integrated animated drop umbilicals. Each umbilical has three size variants and 5 color options, and can be separately moved down up to 15 meters and adjusted horizontally with the deploy limit sliders, and can be turned off as well. The tower also has 8 color options. The tower can be retracted either by manual toggling the animation or by staging.
General animated side-arm style cosmetic hold-down for use with any launch base. Three sizes and two colors are available.
General animated drop-arm style cosmetic hold-down for use with any launch base. Three sizes and two colors are available.
General Hold-Down Type 3: Vert Bolt Flat
General animated flat vertical bolt type cosmetic hold-down for use with any launch base. Three sizes are available, with two heights of the bolt and an optional extended base.
General Hold-Down Type 4: Vert Bolt Tripod
General animated tripod vertical bolt type cosmetic hold-down for use with any launch base. Three sizes are available.
General Hold-Down Type 5: Vert Bolt Arm
General animated vertical bolt arm type cosmetic hold-down for use with any launch base. Three sizes are available.
General Hold-Down Type 6: Clamp Arm Small
General animated small clamp arm type cosmetic hold-down, in classic red and yellow color, for use with any launch base. Three sizes are available.
General Hold-Down Type 7: Clamp Arm Large
General animated large clamp arm type cosmetic hold-down for use with any launch base. Three sizes are available.

Large size General Launch Base, a node-attached launch clamp platform. Has different shapes for 6m and 8m exhaust hole widths. The base frame has 9 color options, and the sides have 3 color options. Optional support pads for hold-downs cane be configured in various ways. The ladder can be toggled in 2 height variants, and the ladder and railings are available in 5 colors. Has manually operated Electric Charge and Fuel Generators, these must be turned on to operate, but can be switched off as well.

Medium size General Launch Base, a node-attached launch clamp platform, with mobile wheel style. Has three different shapes for 4m and 6m exhaust hole widths. The base frame has 9 color options. Optional support pads for hold-downs cane be configured in various ways. The ladders can be toggled in various configurations, and are available in 5 colors. Has manually operated Electric Charge and Fuel Generators, these must be turned on to operate, but can be switched off as well.

Micro size General Launch Base, a node-attached launch clamp platform. Has a two 1.5m wide exhaust holes with square and rectangular shapes, and a 2.5m wide square shape. The base frame has 8 color options. The ladders can be toggled on or off, and are available in 5 colors. Has manually operated Electric Charge and Fuel Generators, these must be turned on to operate, but can be switched off as well.

Mini size General Launch Base, a node-attached launch clamp platform, with mobile wheels or fixed footing styles. Has a 3 shapes of exhaust holes in 1.5m and 2.5m widths, and a 3.5m square hole. The base frame has 8 color options. Optional support pads for hold-downs cane be configured in various ways. The ladders can be toggled in various configurations, and are available in 5 colors. Has manually operated Electric Charge and Fuel Generators, these must be turned on to operate, but can be switched off as well.

Small size General Launch Base, a node-attached launch clamp platform, with mobile wheel style. Has two special exhaust hole variants for the BDB Atlas V and KNES Ariane 5, plus other shapes in 2m, 3m and 4m widths. The base frame has 9 color options, and the side panels have 2 color options. Optional support pads for hold-downs cane be configured in various ways. The ladders can be toggled in various configurations, and are available in 5 colors. Has manually operated Electric Charge and Fuel Generators, these must be turned on to operate, but can be switched off as well.

BIG Extra Large size General Launch Base, a node-attached launch clamp platform. Wider than the Sandbox/Tier 3 launch pad static, the support columns will sit in the ground. Has different shapes for 10m, 14m and 18m exhaust hole widths. The base frame has 9 color options. Optional support pads for hold-downs cane be configured in various ways. The ladders and railings are available in 5 colors. Has manually operated Electric Charge and Fuel Generators, these must be turned on to operate, but can be switched off as well.
Multi-configurable Radial Outward Firing Initiator (ROFI)--"sparker"--for use with all the launch bases. The number of nozzles can be switched between 1, 2 or 3, and has switchable heights.

The core for the Large General Modular Service Tower, containing the base and a 10m tower section. Attach additional tower sections to the top of the towwr. The tower base can be turned off to allow stacking of additional core sections. Available in 8 color options.

A multi-height additional section for the Large General Modular Service Tower, available in 8 colors. Optional side panels in multiple configurations are also available. Use with the General Umbilicals and Swing Arms.
The top plate for the Large General Modular Service Tower. The railings and an optional antenna mast can be toggled on or off.

The core for the Medium General Modular Service Tower, containing the base and a 10m tower section. Attach additional tower sections to the top of the towwr. The tower base can be turned off to allow stacking of additional core sections. Available in 8 color options.

A multi-height additional section for the Medium General Modular Service Tower, available in 8 colors. Optional side panels in multiple configurations are also available. Use with the General Umbilicals and Swing Arms.
The top plate for the Medium General Modular Service Tower. The railings and an optional antenna mast can be toggled on or off.

The core for the Small General Modular Service Tower, containing the base and a 10m tower section. Attach additional tower sections to the top of the towwr. The tower base can be turned off to allow stacking of additional core sections. Available in 8 color options.

A multi-height additional section for the Small General Modular Service Tower, available in 8 colors. Optional side panels in multiple configurations are also available. Use with the General Umbilicals and Swing Arms.
The top plate for the Small General Modular Service Tower. The railings and an optional antenna mast can be toggled on or off.

A large-size fallback-type service tower inspired by the transporter-erector used for the Falcon 9. It has two methods of fallback retraction: A simple one-step type which fully retracts the tower, activated by staging only, and a two-step manual method in which the tower can be first partially retracted by a small amount before launch, followed by a seprate fallback retract for liftoff. The tower has 3 height and 2 color options. The upper clamp has two size options, or can be turned off, and can be adjusted vertically with its deploy limit slider. The fixed umbilicals are moved vertically with the upper clamp, and their length can be adjusted with their deploy limit slider, or turned off.

A very slim and tapered fallback-type service tower. It has two methods of fallback retraction: A simple one-step type which fully retracts the tower, activated by staging only, and a two-step manual method in which the tower can be first partially retracted by a small amount before launch, followed by a seprate fallback retract for liftoff. The tower has only one 15m height option and two color options. The upper clamp has three size options, or can be turned off, and can be adjusted up-and-down with a deploy limit slider. The fixed umbilicals can be adjusted vertically separately from the clamp, and can be adjusted in length with their deploy limit slider, or be turned off.

An even shorter and smaller fallback-type service tower. It has two methods of fallback retraction: A simple one-step type which fully retracts the tower, activated by staging only, and a two-step manual method in which the tower can be first partially retracted by a small amount before launch, followed by a seprate fallback retract for liftoff. The tower has 5 height and two color options. The upper clamp has three size options, or can be turned off, and can be adjusted up-and-down with a deploy limit slider. The fixed umbilicals can be adjusted vertically separately from the clamp, and can be adjusted in length with their deploy limit slider, or be turned off.

A small-size fallback-type service tower inspired by the transporter-erector used for the Falcon 9, but in a shorter, slimmer form. It has two methods of fallback retraction: A simple one-step type which fully retracts the tower, activated by staging only, and a two-step manual method in which the tower can be first partially retracted by a small amount before launch, followed by a seprate fallback retract for liftoff.
